We need to determine SMILES for the molecule given data.

We have molecular formula C9H11O3N. DBE =5. Aromatic carbons count 12? Wait aromatic carbons count 12 but formula only has 9 carbons total. Something inconsistent. Maybe aromatic carbons count 12 refers to aromatic carbons in fragments? The fragments list: 'c1ccc(cc1)' is benzene ring (6 aromatic carbons). 'C(=O)N' is amide carbonyl. 'OC' is methoxy? Actually OC is -O-CH3 (methoxy). Combine fragments: aromatic ring attached to something? Possibly anisamide? Let's think: c1ccc(cc1) is phenyl. C(=O)N is amide carbonyl attached to N. OC is methoxy group. Could be methyl 4-? Wait we need combine fragments to get C9H11O3N. Let's count atoms: phenyl C6H5. C(=O)N adds C1 O1 N1 plus maybe H? That's carbonyl carbon attached to N (amide). OC adds O1 C1 H3 (methoxy). Total C:6+1+1=8? Wait phenyl C6, carbonyl C1, methoxy C1 =8. But formula C9. So missing one carbon maybe linking carbon? Maybe the fragments are separate pieces: phenyl attached to carbonyl (forming benzamide) and OCH3 attached to something else maybe as OCH3 attached to carbonyl (methyl ester) but we have amide not ester. Could be methyl anthranilate? That's methyl 2-aminobenzoate: formula C8H9NO2? Not match.

Let's compute formula for phenyl (C6H5). Add C(=O)N: adds C1 O1 N1 H? The amide group attached to phenyl would be -C(=O)NH2? That would add C1 O1 N1 H2. So total C7 H7? Actually phenyl C6H5 + C1 O1 N1 H2 = C7 H7 O1 N1? Wait H total: 5+2=7. So C7H7NO. Then add OC (methoxy) maybe attached to N? Could be N-methoxy? That would add O1 C1 H3. So total C8 H10 O2 N1? Not match.

Our formula C9H11O3N. Need 9 carbons, 11 H, 3 O, 1 N. DBE 5. Aromatic carbons 12 seems wrong; maybe they meant aromatic carbons count 12? But we only have 6 aromatic carbons in phenyl. Could be two aromatic rings? But formula only 9 carbons, can't have two rings.

Maybe the fragments list includes separate fragments that need to be linked: c1ccc(cc1) (phenyl), C(=O)N (amide), OC (hydroxy methyl). Could be phenyl attached to carbonyl (benzamide) and also OCH3 attached to carbonyl (methyl carbamate) i.e., phenyl carbamate? Actually phenyl carbamate: phenyl-O-CO-NH2 would have phenyl O attached to carbonyl, not carbonyl attached to phenyl. That would have formula C8H9NO2? Not.

Let's think of possible structure: maybe it's methyl 4-aminobenzoate? That is p-aminobenzoic acid methyl ester: formula C8H9NO2? Actually p-aminobenzoic acid (C7H7NO2) plus methyl ester adds CH3O, total C8H9NO2? Not.

Our formula C9H11O3N suggests maybe a phenyl with a carbamate group (O-CO-NH-CH3). That would be phenyl carbamate with methyl on nitrogen: phenyl-O-CO-NH-CH3. Count: phenyl C6H5, O linking to carbonyl O (makes O), carbonyl C1 O1, N1, CH3 attached to N adds C1 H3. Total C8? Wait phenyl C6, carbonyl C1, methyl C1 =8. Need 9 carbons, so maybe also a methoxy attached to phenyl (anisidine). Example: 4-methoxybenzamide? That is anisamide: p-methoxybenzamide. Formula C8? Let's compute: benzamide C7H7NO? Actually benzamide C7H7NO? Wait benzamide C7H7NO? Actually benzamide C7H7NO? Let's compute: C6H5-CO-NH2 => C7H7NO? plus O? carbonyl O already counted. So C7H7NO? plus O? Actually formula C7H7NO? plus O? carbonyl O is O, so C7H7NO? Wait need O1. So C7H7NO? That's C7H7NO? Not correct. Let's compute properly: C6H5 (C6H5) + C=O (C1 O1) + NH2 (N1 H2) => total C7 H7? H5+2=7, O1, N1. So C7H7NO. That's C7H7NO. Add methoxy group OCH3 attached to ring: adds O1 C1 H3. So total C8? Actually C7+1=8 carbons, H7+3=10, O1+1=2, N1. So C8H10NO2. Not match.

Our formula C9H11O3N suggests maybe an extra carbonyl O (two carbonyls) or extra O. Could be phenyl with carbamate (O-CO-NH-CH3) plus extra O? Actually carbamate has two O (one carbonyl O, one alkoxy O). So phenyl-O-CO-NH-CH3 would have phenyl C6H5, carbonyl C1 O1, alkoxy O1, N1, methyl C1 H3. Total C8? C6+1+1=8. Need 9. Maybe also a methoxy on phenyl (adds another C and O). That would be C9, O3, N1, H? phenyl with methoxy and carbamate? That seems too many O.

Let's compute: phenyl (C6H4) if two substituents (since two substituents replace two H). Starting base C6H4. Add methoxy OCH3 (C1 O1 H3). Add carbamate O-CO-NH-CH3 (adds C2? Actually carbonyl C1, O1 carbonyl, O1 linking to phenyl (already counted as phenyl O?), Wait phenyl-O-CO-NH-CH3 attaches via O to phenyl, so phenyl O is part of substituent, not extra carbon. So substituent adds C1 (carbonyl), O1 (carbonyl), N1, CH3 (C1 H3). Also an O linking to phenyl is part of substituent but not extra carbon. So total added carbons: 1 (methoxy) + 1 (carbonyl) +1 (methyl on N) =3. So total C =6+3=9. O count: methoxy O1, carbamate carbonyl O1, linking O1 = total 3 O. N1. Hydrogens: phenyl base C6H4 (since two substituents replace two H) gives H4. Methoxy adds H3. N-methyl adds H3. NH maybe H? The carbamate has NH (one H). So total H =4+3+3+1=11. That matches C9H11O3N! Good.

Thus structure is 4-methoxy phenyl carbamate? Actually phenyl with two substituents: one methoxy (OCH3) and one carbamate O-CO-NH-CH3 attached via O to phenyl (i.e., phenyl-O-CO-NH-CH3 is phenyl carbamate). So overall is anisyl methylcarbamate? Wait anisyl is methoxy phenyl. So anisyl methylcarbamate (4-methoxy phenyl methylcarbamate) maybe.

SMILES: For para? Not specified orientation. Could be any position. But fragments list: c1ccc(cc1) (phenyl) plus C(=O)N (amide) plus OC (methoxy). The linking likely: phenyl attached to carbonyl via O? Actually fragments: OC is methoxy group (maybe attached to phenyl). C(=O)N is carbonyl attached to N. So combine: phenyl-O-CO-N-? Actually need O linking phenyl to carbonyl, which is not in fragments list. But we have OC (methoxy) maybe attached to phenyl as OCH3. So phenyl has two O substituents: one OCH3, one O-CO-NH-CH3. The latter includes carbonyl and N and methyl (CH3) not shown? Actually C(=O)N fragment includes carbonyl carbon attached to N, but missing methyl on N. Could be N-methyl? Not in fragments. But formula includes methyl on N (CH3). That could be part of OC? No.

Maybe the N-methyl is part of OC? Actually OC could be O-CH3 attached to N (N-OC)? But OC is just O attached to C (methoxy). Could be N-OC (N-O-CH3) but not typical.

Alternative: The structure could be phenyl carbamate with methyl on nitrogen: phenyl-O-CO-NH-CH3 (methylcarbamate). That includes OCH3? No, the methyl is on N, not O. So we have only one methoxy group (the N-methyl). But we also have a methoxy substituent on phenyl (OC). So two OCH3 groups: one attached to phenyl, one attached to N? That would give O3? Let's count: phenyl-O-CO-N-CH3 (N-methyl) has O linking phenyl, carbonyl O, total O2. No methoxy on phenyl. But we need O3, so need extra OCH3 somewhere. So likely phenyl has methoxy substituent, and the carbamate N is methyl (N-CH3). That matches O3.

Thus SMILES: For para orientation: COc1ccc(OCOC)cc1? Wait OCOC is O-CO-NCH3? Actually O-CO-NCH3 is O C(=O)N C. So phenyl-O-CO-NC. So SMILES: COc1ccc(OCOC)cc1? Let's construct: phenyl with methoxy at position 1 (CO-). Another substituent O-CO-NC (carbamate). So SMILES: COc1ccc(OCOC)cc1? But OCOC is O-C(=O)-N-C? Need carbonyl: O C(=O) N C. So O C(=O) N C. So O C(=O) N C. So O C(=O) N C. So O C(=O) N C. So O C(=O) N C. So O C(=O) N C. So the group is O C(=O) N C. So SMILES: O C(=O) N C. So combined: COc1ccc(O C(=O) N C)cc1. Need to ensure correct connectivity: O attached to aromatic carbon, then carbonyl carbon, then N, then methyl.

Thus final SMILES: COc1ccc(O C(=O)NC)cc1. Remove spaces: COc1ccc(OC(=O)NC)cc1.
